1.h: What makes a penetration test legal

blocks.x: A penetration test is authorised, ethical hacking done to find weaknesses **before** a real attacker does. The single thing that separates it from a crime is **written authorization** — a signed contract or statement of work from the owner of the systems being tested. No matter how good your intent, testing systems without that permission is illegal. On the job and on the exam, the first instinct for any scenario is always: *are we scoped and authorised for this?*
The **Rules of Engagement** define the boundaries of the test:
**Scope** — exactly which systems, networks and applications may be tested. Anything outside scope is off-limits, even if you find a way in.
**Timing** — when testing may happen (often a maintenance window).
**Permitted and forbidden techniques** — high-impact actions like **denial-of-service, social engineering and physical intrusion** are usually forbidden unless explicitly authorised.
**Points of contact and a stop procedure** — so the client can halt testing immediately if something breaks.
A "get out of jail free" letter is the written authorisation you carry proving the work is sanctioned — it documents permission, it does not excuse acting outside scope.
Testing cloud-hosted or shared systems may also require the **provider's** permission.

If you discover a path into an **out-of-scope** system, you stop, document it, and notify the client — you continue only if scope is formally amended in writing. Scope applies at **every** phase, from recon to reporting.

A structured methodology keeps a test thorough and repeatable. The typical phases: 1. **Planning** — scoping, ROE, legal. 2. **Reconnaissance** — gather information about the target. 3. **Scanning / Enumeration** — find live hosts, ports, services and detail. 4. **Exploitation** — prove a vulnerability is real within scope. 5. **Post-exploitation** — situational awareness, escalation, lateral movement. 6. **Reporting** — the deliverable that creates value. Knowing the order matters on the exam: you *enumerate before you exploit*, and you *report at the end*.
Testers use shared frameworks so results are consistent and defensible:
**MITRE ATT&CK** — a catalogue of real adversary tactics and techniques (TTPs), used to plan and describe attacks.
**The Cyber Kill Chain** — the stages of an attack from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.
**PTES, OSSTMM, NIST 800-115** — penetration-testing/assessment methodologies.
**OWASP Testing Guide / Top 10** — the reference for web application testing.
A standard pen test aims for broad **coverage** of vulnerabilities.
**Red teaming** emulates a real adversary to test the defenders' detection and response, often stealthy and goal-based.
**Assumed breach** testing starts from the premise that an attacker already has a foothold, focusing on lateral movement and detection rather than initial access.
Documenting your methodology in the report makes findings reproducible and shows what was and wasn't covered.

Reconnaissance is gathering information about the target, and **passive** recon does it **without directly touching** the target's systems — so it is low-risk and stealthy. It relies on **OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence)**: public data anyone can access. Early passive recon builds a picture of the attack surface without alerting anyone.
**WHOIS** — domain registration details, registrar, and name servers.
**DNS records** — subdomains, mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), text records (TXT).
**Certificate Transparency logs** (e.g. crt.sh) — publicly list issued certificates, often revealing subdomains.
**Google dorking** — advanced search operators (`site:`, `filetype:`, `intitle:`) that surface exposed files or logins.
**Social media and job posts** — employees, roles, and the exact technologies in use (job ads often leak the tech stack).

The key distinction for the exam: passive recon uses only public data and sends nothing to the target; **active** recon (scanning) directly interacts with target systems and can be detected. You gather all you can passively first, then move to active techniques on authorised, in-scope hosts. Organisations reduce their own exposure by privacy-protecting WHOIS, minimising info in job posts, and reviewing what CT logs reveal.

Once passive recon is done, **active** scanning directly probes authorised, in-scope hosts to discover what's there. **Nmap** (Network Mapper) is the standard tool — it finds live hosts, open ports and the services behind them. Run it only on systems you own or are authorised to test.
`-sS` — a **SYN (half-open)** scan: fast and relatively stealthy because it doesn't complete the full handshake (needs privileges).
`-sV` — **version detection**, identifying the software and version on each open port so you can match it to known vulnerabilities.
`-O` — **OS fingerprinting**, guessing the operating system from network-stack behaviour.
`-sC` — run the **default NSE scripts** for extra discovery (banner grabbing, common checks).
`-sU` — a **UDP** scan (slower and more ambiguous because UDP is connectionless; still needed for DNS, SNMP, DHCP).
`-Pn` — skip host discovery and treat the host as online (useful when ICMP is blocked).
**Timing templates** `-T0`–`-T5` trade speed for stealth/load: `-T4` is fast, `-T1` is slow and quiet (gentler on fragile targets).
`-p-` scans **all** 65,535 TCP ports; `-F` scans a fast common set.
`-oA basename` saves output in all formats for later parsing and comparison. A UDP result of "open|filtered" means no reply — it could be open or dropped, which is why UDP scanning is less certain.

**Enumeration** goes deeper than scanning: it actively extracts detailed information — users, shares, versions, configuration — from the services a scan found. It turns "port 445 is open" into "these shares and these users exist." Thorough enumeration is what separates a professional from a script kiddie, because precise detail makes later exploitation reliable and reduces the risk of causing damage.
**SMB (445)** — shares, users and OS details when misconfigured (tools query shares and null sessions where allowed).
**Web servers** — **content discovery** (directory brute-forcing) with wordlist tools finds hidden endpoints like `/admin` or `/backup`.
**SNMP** — a default community string ("public") can leak system info, interfaces and running processes.
**DNS** — a misconfigured server may allow a **zone transfer (AXFR)** that dumps every record — a finding in itself.
**LDAP** — anonymous binds can expose directory users, groups and structure.

5.h: Banner grabbing and why detail matters

blocks.x: **Banner grabbing** retrieves the identification string a service returns, revealing its software and version — which map directly to known CVEs. The reason to enumerate thoroughly *before* exploiting is control: you exploit precisely, quietly, and without breaking things, because you understand exactly what you're dealing with.

A **vulnerability scanner** checks targets against a database of known weaknesses and misconfigurations, then reports likely issues. It **reports**, it doesn't exploit — a tester validates the findings afterward. Scanners save huge time but must be used carefully: an aggressive scan can crash fragile production services, so intensity and timing are agreed in the ROE.
**Authenticated (credentialed) scanning** logs in to check patch levels and configuration, giving far deeper and more accurate results than an unauthenticated scan.
A **false positive** is a reported vulnerability that isn't actually exploitable; validation separates real issues from noise.
Raw scanner output is **not** a professional report — findings must be validated and prioritised first.
**CVSS** scores severity from 0.0 to 10.0 (9.0+ is Critical); real risk also depends on **exposure** and business impact.
A **CVE** is the unique public identifier for a known vulnerability.
**Compliance scanning** checks systems against a benchmark (CIS, PCI DSS) and reports configuration gaps.
The workflow is: scan, **validate** the important findings by hand (e.g. grab the real version banner), then prioritise.

A pile of scanner output isn't useful until you turn it into risk-ranked, actionable results. Real-world risk depends on **severity AND exposure/exploitability AND business impact** — a critical CVE on an isolated box may rank *below* a medium flaw on an internet-facing app. Mapping findings to **business impact** ("this exposes customer PII") is what motivates leadership to fix them.
**Chaining** combines several lower-severity issues into one high-impact result — e.g. an information leak + a weak password + a misconfiguration = full compromise.

An **attack path** in the report shows the steps from initial access to the objective, so defenders can see the cheapest place to break the chain — often a single well-placed control stops the whole thing.

Each finding needs a clear **remediation** — specific, actionable guidance, not "be more secure." Prioritise findings (P1–P4) by severity, exposure and impact so the client fixes the most dangerous issues first. Don't list only "critical" items — chained lows and quick wins matter too. When a client knowingly chooses to live with a risk, that's a documented **risk acceptance**, recorded with who accepted it. The report, not the number of shells, is what delivers value.

In a pen test, exploitation exists to **demonstrate the real impact** of a vulnerability within the authorised scope — not to cause maximum damage. You produce a **proof of concept (PoC)** that turns a theoretical finding into a confirmed one, then document it and clean up. The professional mindset is "do no harm": prove the risk with the lowest-impact method, and always confirm the target is in scope before firing an exploit.
**Metasploit** is a framework that organises exploits and payloads:
An **exploit** module abuses a specific vulnerability; a **payload** is the code that runs on the target afterward (for example a shell).
A **reverse shell** connects *from* the target back to the tester's listener (useful when the target can't accept inbound connections); a **bind shell** does the opposite.
Payloads can be **staged** (delivered in stages, smaller initially) or **stageless** (self-contained).
`search`, `use`, `set RHOSTS`, and `run` are the typical flow; always read a module's description and impact first.

Before running any exploit, understand what it does so you don't cause an outage — untrusted PoC code can be destructive or backdoored, so test in a lab first. After a successful PoC, **document** the evidence (host, timestamp, steps, screenshot, impact) and **clean up** anything you left behind — test accounts, files, implants. Prove it, record it, restore the system.
Password attacks in a test show how weak credentials really are, always within scope and ROE (lockouts and account access can disrupt real users). Two broad approaches:
**Offline cracking** works on captured **hashes** without touching the live system — no lockouts, limited only by compute and hash strength.
**Online attacks** try credentials against the live service and must respect lockout policy.
A **dictionary attack** tries passwords from a wordlist (like rockyou.txt); **brute force** tries every combination.
**Password spraying** tries one common password across many accounts to stay under per-account lockout thresholds.
**Pass-the-hash** authenticates using a captured hash without cracking it.
Tools: **hashcat** (GPU-accelerated, many hash types) and **John the Ripper** (CPU-based) crack hashes offline.

A strong, **salted, slow** hash (bcrypt/argon2) resists cracking: the salt defeats precomputation (rainbow tables) and the slowness limits guesses per second. Fast, unsalted hashes (MD5) fall quickly. The remediations a tester recommends are the same defences: **MFA**, long passphrases, account lockout/rate limiting, banning breached passwords, and slow salted hashing server-side.
Web apps are a huge attack surface, tested against the **OWASP Top 10**. The classics:
**SQL injection** — user input concatenated into a database query, letting the attacker run their own SQL. Fixed with **parameterized queries**.

**Cross-site scripting (XSS)** — injecting script that runs in a victim's browser; **stored** XSS is saved on the server and served to many, **reflected** bounces off a single request. Fixed with output encoding and a CSP.
**IDOR / broken access control** — changing an ID in a request exposes another user's data because authorization isn't enforced per object.
**CSRF** — tricking a browser into sending an authenticated request the user didn't intend; defended with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
**SSRF** — abusing a server to make requests to internal systems the attacker can't reach directly (often to steal cloud metadata credentials).
**Command injection** — passing user input to a system shell without sanitisation.

A **proxy tool** like **Burp Suite** or **OWASP ZAP** intercepts, inspects and modifies HTTP requests between the browser and the app — the core of manual web testing. You can also test purely from the command line with `curl` and fuzz parameters with `ffuf`. For each finding, name the OWASP category and give a concrete defence — the common thread is again "never trust user input; treat it as data, not code."
On the authorised network, testers demonstrate the risk of weak protocols and configurations:

An **on-path (MITM)** position lets you observe and possibly modify traffic between two hosts — proving why unencrypted protocols (Telnet, FTP, HTTP) are dangerous, since credentials and data can be captured.
**SMB relay** abuses authentication being relayed to a host that trusts it; **SMB signing** and disabling legacy auth mitigate it.
**LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning** works because Windows falls back to these name-resolution protocols that an attacker can answer, capturing hashes; disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS removes the path.
A service using **plaintext** is a finding on its own — recommend encrypted replacements (SSH, SFTP, HTTPS, LDAPS).
**SNMP** with a default/writable community string can leak or even change device configuration; recommend SNMPv3 with auth+privacy.
**DoS-style tests** can take down production and are usually out of scope unless explicitly authorised.

The recommendations that come out of network testing are consistent: **encrypt everything in transit**, **segment** the network so a foothold can't reach every zone, disable legacy name-resolution and enable SMB signing, and use SNMPv3. Encryption makes captured traffic useless; segmentation limits lateral movement.

12.h: Testing Wi-Fi (only what you own or are authorised for)

blocks.x: Wireless testing is legal only on networks you own or have explicit written authorisation for — deauth and injection against others' Wi-Fi is illegal. The goal is to show weak wireless security and recommend fixes.
**WEP** is a finding because its broken cipher/IV scheme can be cracked in minutes — recommend WPA2-AES at minimum, ideally **WPA3**.
Capturing a **WPA2 handshake** allows *offline* passphrase cracking — but a long, random passphrase makes this impractical.
An **evil twin** (a rogue AP impersonating a trusted SSID) shows the risk of users connecting to fake networks.
**WPS** is a finding because its PIN can be brute-forced to recover the passphrase — recommend disabling it.
**Monitor mode** on a wireless adapter is needed to capture raw 802.11 frames; not all adapters support it, so an external USB adapter is often required.
**WPA2/3-Enterprise (802.1X)** authenticates each user via RADIUS instead of a shared key, so credentials are individually revocable.

The remediation after a wireless assessment is real controls, not obscurity: **WPA3 (or WPA2-AES)** with a strong passphrase, WPS disabled, separate guest/IoT VLANs, and a wireless IDS to detect rogue/evil-twin APs.
Cloud testing focuses on the customer-owned layers, since the provider owns the rest (shared responsibility). The most common findings:
**Public storage buckets** exposing data — check bucket ACLs/policies first.
**Over-privileged IAM roles** — a compromised credential inherits far more access than needed; least privilege limits the blast radius.
The **metadata service** (e.g. 169.254.169.254) can be abused via **SSRF** to retrieve temporary role credentials; IMDSv2 and blocking SSRF mitigate this.
A **container escape** breaks out of a container to the host, defeating isolation; non-root containers, seccomp/AppArmor and avoiding `--privileged` reduce it.
**Hard-coded secrets** in an image or repo are a finding — anyone with the image gets the credentials; use a secrets manager and scan images.
Enumerating cloud **IAM** during a test finds excessive permissions and privilege-escalation paths (role/trust chaining).

The fixes after a cloud test are consistent: **least-privilege IAM**, **block public storage**, **enable logging/monitoring**, use **IMDSv2**, and harden containers (non-root, minimal image, no baked-in secrets, scanned for CVEs). Stay within the authorised, customer-owned scope unless the provider authorises more.

14.h: Testing the human and physical layers

blocks.x: People and buildings are part of the attack surface, and testing them is ethical **only** when explicitly authorised in the ROE with agreed limits and care for staff wellbeing. The goal is improvement, not punishment.
A **phishing simulation** measures how many users click versus report, to improve training and controls — the landing page teaches, it doesn't harvest real credentials.
A **pretext** is a believable cover story used to gain trust (posing as IT support).
**Vishing** (phone) might try to get staff to reveal info or reset credentials; recommend callback verification.
Capturing metrics (click rate and, importantly, **report rate**) baselines behaviour; a rising report rate shows a healthier security culture.
**Tailgating** (following staff through a secure door) demonstrates weak access control — recommend mantraps and badge discipline.
**Baiting** with a dropped USB tests whether staff plug in unknown devices — recommend disabling autorun plus training.

The strongest defence a tester can recommend against social engineering is ongoing **awareness training** plus **verification procedures** and **MFA** — because people are the target, so empowering and training them is what actually works.

Once you gain authorised access to a host, the first job is **situational awareness**, not immediate further attack. You answer: *who am I, where am I, what can I reach?* On Linux, `id` and `whoami` reveal your account context and whether you have elevated rights; `sudo -l` shows what you may run as root. Enumerate the local host — users, groups, running services, scheduled tasks (`cron`), network connections — before acting.

The foothold changes what's reachable: internal hosts and services that were invisible from outside may now be accessible, opening the way to lateral movement. Checking scheduled tasks and writable files owned by root reveals privilege-escalation opportunities (and sometimes existing malware).
**Living off the land** means using built-in system tools rather than dropping detectable malware — smaller footprint, harder to detect.
**Document every command** you run: for the report, for reproducibility, and to enable full cleanup afterward.
Limit activity to what's necessary to demonstrate impact within scope — prove the risk, then stop. A scoped, justified, reversible next step is the professional standard.
After landing as a low-privilege user, the goal is to become **root**, then document the path and its fix. Classic checks:
**SUID binaries** — `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` lists programs that run with their owner's (often root's) privileges; some can be abused (cross-reference **GTFOBins**).
**`sudo -l`** — shows what you may run as root; a misconfigured `NOPASSWD` entry can be an instant escalation.
**Writable root cron scripts** — a script run by root that you can edit lets you run commands as root.
**Outdated kernel** — a known local kernel exploit.
**Path hijacking** — a privileged program calling a binary by name with an attacker-controlled PATH; fix with absolute paths.
**File capabilities** (`getcap`) — a binary with `cap_setuid` can escalate without the SUID bit.

Enumeration scripts (linpeas-style) automate these checks — SUID, sudo, cron, kernel, writable files, credentials in configs — but you still verify manually to avoid false positives. After demonstrating escalation, capture proof (`id` showing `uid=0`), then **remediate and clean up** any changes. A typical finding + fix reads: "world-writable script run by root as cron → local root; fix: `chown root:root`, `chmod 700`, audit the cron directory."
On Windows the escalation paths differ but the mindset is the same — find a misconfiguration that grants SYSTEM. Common checks:

**Service misconfigurations** — services running as SYSTEM with weak permissions: an **unquoted service path** with spaces lets a planted binary run as SYSTEM; a **writable service binary** or weak service ACLs do the same.
**AlwaysInstallElevated** — if enabled, any user can install an MSI as SYSTEM.
**Access tokens** — certain privileges (like `SeImpersonate`) enable token-impersonation escalation.
**Stored credentials** in the registry or files can be reused for higher-privilege accounts.
**DLL hijacking** — a privileged process loading a DLL from a writable location.
`whoami /priv` shows your privileges (look for `SeImpersonatePrivilege`); tools like **WinPEAS** or **PowerUp** automate the checks.
After demonstrating escalation, capture proof and then remediate/clean up.

The remediations you recommend improve credential hygiene: **LAPS** for unique local admin passwords, no plaintext credentials in scripts/registry, least privilege with separate admin accounts, and enabling protections like Credential Guard.
A single foothold is rarely the objective — you show how far an attacker could get.
**Lateral movement** is using a compromised host to reach and compromise **other** in-scope systems.

**Pivoting** is routing your traffic *through* a compromised host to reach networks you otherwise couldn't — for example a DMZ foothold used to reach the internal LAN (in scope). An SSH dynamic port-forward (`ssh -D`) plus a SOCKS proxy is a common technique.
**Pass-the-hash** and **pass-the-ticket** reuse captured credentials/tickets to authenticate to other hosts without cracking passwords.
**Credential dumping** harvests reusable credentials to move on.
A **jump/pivot host** reachable to many segments is high value — compromising it grants broad reach.

The key defence against lateral movement is **network segmentation/microsegmentation**, so one foothold can't freely reach other zones. Add **unique local admin passwords (LAPS)** and **SMB signing** to stop credential reuse, least privilege and tiered admin, MFA on admin access, and EDR/monitoring for credential dumping and anomalous logons. Everything stays strictly in scope — reaching out-of-scope or third-party systems is illegal.

**Persistence** is how an attacker keeps access. In an authorised test you demonstrate it only if it's in scope, and — crucially — **everything you add must be documented and removed at the end**. Testing persistence also measures the client's detection (a purple-team benefit).
**Linux** persistence: cron jobs, systemd services, SSH `authorized_keys`, modified startup scripts.
**Windows** persistence: scheduled tasks, services, registry Run keys, startup folders.
Defenders monitor exactly these locations for unexpected changes.
**Cleanup** at the end of an engagement means removing every tool, account, implant and change you introduced, restoring systems to their prior state and confirming with the client.
**Never delete the client's logs** — those are the client's evidence needed for detection review. Attackers clear logs; ethical testers preserve them and note their own activity.
Leaving hidden access would be unethical and dangerous, so a persistence finding in the report includes how it was established and how to detect and remove similar techniques.

For each technique, note how a defender would catch it — cron/systemd changes via file-integrity monitoring and config audits; an `authorized_keys` change via key-addition alerts and EDR; beaconing via flow analysis. Testing whether your actions were detected is the purple-team value: undetected TTPs are exactly what the client needs to know about.

The most valuable output of a penetration test is a **clear, prioritized report** with findings, evidence, impact and remediation — not the exploit code or a raw scanner dump. The report is what drives fixes and creates value.
An **executive summary** for non-technical leadership: overall risk, business impact, and key recommendations, in business terms.
Each **technical finding** includes: description, affected assets, **severity**, **evidence** (screenshots, timestamps), **impact**, and a specific, actionable **remediation**.
Findings are **ranked by risk** so the client fixes the most dangerous issues first — prioritisation turns a list into an action plan.
Handle sensitive report data (credentials, exploit detail) securely, sharing only with authorised parties.
Critical, actively exploitable findings should be **communicated promptly** during the engagement, not held until the final report.
**Retesting** after remediation confirms the fixes actually resolved each finding.

A remediation must be specific ("use parameterized queries; least-privilege DB account; input validation"), not vague ("be more secure") — a developer should be able to fix it from your write-up alone.
Nmap's real power for enumeration is the **NSE**, a library of hundreds of scripts organised into categories. On authorised targets:
`-sC` (or `--script=default`) runs the safe default scripts for extra detail.
Category and named scripts target specific services: `--script http-methods,http-title` on web ports, `--script smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users` on SMB, `--script ftp-anon` to check anonymous FTP.
**Avoid** the `intrusive`/`dos` categories on fragile production without explicit permission — they can disrupt services.
`-oA basename` writes normal, XML and grepable output at once, so you can parse and **diff** scans later (`ndiff scan1.xml scan2.xml` shows what changed).
`-p-` scans all ports; combine a full service+script scan and save everything: `nmap -sS -sV -sC -p- -oA fullscan <ip>`.
Parse grepable output with `awk`/`grep` to build a clean host/service inventory for the report.

Good testers script their recon: a small bash script that takes an IP and runs host discovery, a version scan, and default scripts — saving each stage — turns a repeatable process into one command. NSE plus saved, parseable output is how you enumerate thoroughly and document precisely, which is the foundation for reliable exploitation.
Frameworks are convenient, but a good tester can exploit and manage access with basic tools, which also helps in restricted environments.

**Netcat (nc)** is the "swiss army knife": `nc -lvnp 4444` starts a **listener** on your attacker machine (`-l` listen, `-v` verbose, `-n` no DNS, `-p` port), waiting for a target to connect back for a reverse shell (authorised labs only).
A **reverse shell** connects from the target to your listener — it traverses many firewalls that block inbound — while a **bind shell** listens on the target.
A raw shell breaks on interactive prompts and Ctrl+C. **Upgrade a "dumb" shell to a full TTY** so you get job control, tab completion and reliable interactive tools:
`python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'`, then background with Ctrl+Z and run `stty raw -echo; fg` for a proper terminal.
Move files with a quick HTTP server: `python3 -m http.server 8000` on the attacker, then `wget`/`curl` on the target; or use netcat both ways.
`searchsploit <service> <version>` searches the local Exploit-DB copy for a PoC.

Before running any public exploit, **read and understand what it does and test it in a lab** — untrusted exploit code can be destructive or backdoored. You can also drive web exploits purely with `curl`, demonstrating issues like IDOR or SQL injection from the command line.

On Windows networks, **Active Directory (AD)** is the crown jewel — compromising it can grant control over the entire domain, and therefore most corporate resources. Testing it stays strictly authorised and scoped, because domain-wide actions can disrupt the whole organisation.
**Kerberoasting** — requesting service accounts' Kerberos tickets and cracking them offline for their passwords; defended with long (25+ char) service-account passwords or gMSA.
**AS-REP roasting** — targeting accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled; enable pre-auth and use strong passwords.
**Pass-the-ticket** — reusing Kerberos tickets to authenticate as a user without their password.
**Golden ticket** — forging a Kerberos TGT using the `krbtgt` hash for broad, persistent access; rotating the `krbtgt` password (twice) invalidates forged tickets.
**BloodHound** collects AD relationships (sessions, group memberships, ACLs, trusts) and graphs the shortest **attack path** to Domain Admin, so you target the weakest edge.
Enumeration tools (`enum4linux`, LDAP queries) reveal domain users, groups and structure.

The AD hardening you recommend: a **tiered admin** model (separate Domain Admin accounts not used daily), **LAPS**, strong/gMSA service accounts, MFA on admin access, disabling legacy protocols, and monitoring for Kerberoasting and DCSync.

Automation brings consistency, speed and fewer errors across many targets — turning a repeatable process into one command. But a buggy script can hit out-of-scope hosts or cause load at scale, so add **scope checks** and rate limits, and test scripts first.
Loop over targets: `for ip in $(cat targets.txt); do ping -c1 -W1 $ip >/dev/null && echo "$ip up"; done`.
Parse output: `grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' scan.txt | sort -u` extracts unique IPs; `awk '/445\/open/{print $2}'` pulls hosts with a port open.
Decode data: `base64 -d` decodes captured strings; a Python one-liner URL-encodes or decodes payloads.
A no-tools port check: `bash -c 'echo > /dev/tcp/host/22 && echo open'`.

Keep tool output **structured** (JSON/CSV/XML) so it's easy to parse, diff and feed into the report. A scoped sweep script should refuse any IP outside the authorised range before scanning. And automate **evidence collection** — a script that timestamps and saves `id`, `ss`, `ps` and `sudo -l` on a foothold captures reproducible proof for the report in one command.
Databases and APIs hold the data attackers ultimately want, so they get focused testing on authorised systems.
**Weak or default database credentials** (e.g. `root` with no/weak password) are a frequent, high-impact way in — connect with the DB client and enumerate contents (`SHOW DATABASES;`).
**SQL injection** can extract schema and data — e.g. a `UNION SELECT` against `information_schema` reveals table names; the fix is always parameterized queries plus a least-privilege DB account.
**Missing authentication** — endpoints that return data without requiring a login.
**Broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR)** — changing an ID lets one user access another's objects; enforce per-object authorization server-side.
**Verbose errors** — full stack traces leak internal details; return generic messages.
**No rate limiting** — enables brute-force and credential stuffing; add rate limiting, lockout and MFA.
Interact with APIs using `curl` (`-i` to see headers and status, `-X POST` with a JSON body), checking auth, input handling and error verbosity.

The remediations tie together: require authentication and per-object authorization, rate-limit sensitive endpoints, return generic errors, validate input, use parameterized queries, and run the database under a least-privilege account. Each recommendation maps directly to an observed weakness so developers can act on it.

In an authorised test, understanding evasion helps you assess how well the client **detects and responds** — the goal is better detection, not staying permanently hidden. This is the purple-team purpose.
Attackers **live off the land** (LOLBins), using built-in tools like PowerShell or `certutil` to avoid dropping detectable malware.
**Timestomping** alters file timestamps to hinder forensics.
**Obfuscating/encoding** payloads evades signature-based detection — but behaviour-based **EDR** is harder to evade.
**Beaconing** to command-and-control shows up as regular, periodic connections to an unusual destination.
When a technique is **not** detected, you report the **detection gap** so the client can add monitoring. For each technique you tested, give the detection the client should have:
LOLBins → EDR command-line and parent/child process alerts.
Log tampering → central/immutable logs plus integrity monitoring; alert on log-clearing events.
Beaconing → NetFlow analysis and threat-intel matching.

The best defensive recommendation is depth: **centralized logging + EDR + behaviour analytics + tuned alerts**. Detection depth matters more than any single tool, and forwarding logs off-host in real time stops an attacker quietly erasing evidence.
A tester should know the core toolkit, what each tool does, and its basic syntax, so you reach for the right one instantly:
**nmap** — network/service discovery (`nmap -sV <target>`).
**gobuster / ffuf** — web content discovery and fuzzing (`gobuster dir -u http://<t> -w <wordlist>`; `ffuf -u http://<t>/FUZZ -w <wordlist>`).
**hashcat / John the Ripper** — offline hash cracking (`hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt <wordlist>` where `-m` picks the hash type).
**Burp Suite / OWASP ZAP** — intercept and modify web traffic.
**Wireshark / tcpdump** — capture and analyse packets.
**BloodHound** — map Active Directory attack paths.
**searchsploit** — search the local Exploit-DB.

Real work chains tools together: `nmap` finds an open web port → `gobuster` discovers a hidden endpoint → `curl` interacts with that specific vulnerable endpoint. Keeping a **personal cheat sheet** of your ten most-used commands, with a one-line note each, means you can recall them under time pressure — which matters both on the job and on the exam's performance-based questions.

The Pentest+ exam includes **performance-based questions (PBQs)** that require you to analyse tool output, choose or complete commands, or work through a scenario — so hands-on command familiarity is exactly what wins points. As with any timed exam, **flag** the slow PBQs, secure the quick multiple-choice points first, then return.
When asked for the **NEXT step** in a methodology, choose the one that logically follows the phase order — you *enumerate before you exploit*, and you *report at the end*.
When given **tool output**, read it carefully and pick the action it actually supports.
The professional's first consideration in any scenario is **scope and authorisation** — that instinct is almost always the right answer.
When two exploits both work, the safest choice is the **lower-impact** one that proves the risk without disrupting the target.

Every engagement — and the exam — comes back to a clear, prioritised **report** with evidence and remediation, which is what creates value for the client. Combine that with the phase order, the right tool for each task, and an unwavering commitment to staying in scope and doing no harm, and you have the mindset the certification is really testing. Practising the labs and command drills alongside this theory is what builds the hands-on confidence the PBQs reward.
